contexte: PedalPoint rents bikes from five STORE locations in the United Kingdom (Bristol, Edinburgh, Brighton, Manchester and Keswick). Each BIKE belongs to one store and to one CATEGORY (city bike, electric bike, mountain bike, road bike, kids bike, cargo bike), which sets its standard daily rate. When a CUSTOMER picks up bikes in a store, a RENTAL is recorded (start date, store, customer); its return date stays empty until the bikes are brought back. A rental can include several bikes: each one is a RENTAL_LINE with the daily price actually charged (10 % off for rentals of 5 days or more). A customer may have been referred by another customer (ReferredBy). Dates are stored as 'yyyy-mm-dd'.
source: Demonstration exercise for SQL Lab. Entirely fictitious company and data.

questions.enonce: Display the list of bike categories offered by PedalPoint (all columns).
questions.indice: The star * displays every column of a table.

questions.enonce: Display the last name, first name and phone number of the customers who live in Bristol, sorted alphabetically by last name.
questions.indice: A condition on a text value is written between single quotes: City = 'Bristol'. Sorting is done with ORDER BY.

cinema.+select: The email is not displayed, even though the filter is on it: a column can be used in the WHERE without appearing in the SELECT.
cinema.+filtres: « Have not given an email address » means the cell is **empty** (NULL), not an empty text. `Email = NULL` never returns anything, because NULL is equal to nothing, not even to NULL: only `IS NULL` works.
cinema.+resultat: Check: 5 customers out of 25 (Martin, Hughes, Murphy, Thompson and Ali). The opposite question (customers who did give an email) would use `IS NOT NULL`.

questions.enonce: Display the customers (number, last name, first name, phone) who have not given an email address.
questions.indice: A missing value is tested with IS NULL (not with = NULL).

questions.enonce: Display the bikes (number, model, brand) with a large frame (frame size 'L'), sorted by brand.
questions.indice: Two clauses: WHERE to keep the large frames, ORDER BY to sort the result.

cinema.+select: No GROUP BY here: the three functions work on the whole table and each returns **a single value**, so the result is one row with three columns. Naming them with AS (`AVG(DailyRate) AS AverageRate`) makes the result easier to read.
cinema.+resultat: Check: average 25.83, minimum 10 (Kids bike), maximum 40 (Cargo bike). This is the average of the 6 categories, not of the bikes: a category with many bikes counts no more than a category with few.

questions.enonce: Display the average, the lowest and the highest standard daily rate of the bike categories.
questions.indice: The functions AVG (average), MIN and MAX each return a single value for the whole table.

questions.enonce: Display the rentals (number, start date, return date) that started in April 2025.
questions.indice: Combine MONTH() and YEAR(), or use BETWEEN with two dates.

questions.enonce: Display the number of rentals per year (year, number of rentals), based on the start date.
questions.indice: You can group on the result of a function: GROUP BY YEAR(StartDate).

cinema.+select: DATEDIFF(end, start): the **later** date comes first. Reversed, `DATEDIFF(StartDate, ReturnDate)` gives a negative number, and the filter `>= 7` would keep nothing.
cinema.+filtres: « Returned rentals »: no extra condition is needed. A rental not yet returned has an empty ReturnDate, so DATEDIFF gives NULL, and NULL >= 7 is never true: rentals 1036, 1037 and 1038 are left out automatically. Adding `AND ReturnDate IS NOT NULL` would also be correct, just redundant.
cinema.+tri: Variant accepted: name the column `AS Duration` in the SELECT, then sort with `ORDER BY Duration DESC`.
cinema.+resultat: Check: 5 rentals, two of 10 days (1006, 1017) and three of exactly 7 days (1018, 1019, 1030). With `> 7` instead of `>= 7`, those three would disappear.

questions.enonce: Display the returned rentals that lasted 7 days or more: rental number, start date, return date and duration in days, from the longest to the shortest.
correction: SELECT RentalId, StartDate, ReturnDate, DATEDIFF(ReturnDate, StartDate)
variantes: SELECT RentalId, StartDate, ReturnDate, DATEDIFF(ReturnDate, StartDate) AS Duration
questions.indice: DATEDIFF(end, start) returns the number of days between two dates. A rental that is not returned yet has no return date, so DATEDIFF gives no value for it.

questions.enonce: Display the bikes of the Lakeside store (store number 5): bike number, model and category name.
variantes: INNER JOIN CATEGORY ON BIKE.CategoryId = CATEGORY.CategoryId
questions.indice: The category name is in CATEGORY: link BIKE and CATEGORY with CategoryId (foreign key of BIKE).

questions.enonce: Display, without duplicates, the model and brand of the bikes rented in rentals that started in May 2025.
variantes: INNER JOIN RENTAL_LINE ON BIKE.BikeId = RENTAL_LINE.BikeId
INNER JOIN RENTAL ON RENTAL_LINE.RentalId = RENTAL.RentalId
questions.indice: The model is in BIKE and the start date in RENTAL, but these two tables are not linked directly: RENTAL_LINE (one line per bike rented) connects them. It must appear in the FROM even though none of its columns is displayed.

cinema.+tables: « Electric bike (category number 2) »: the category number is already in BIKE (CategoryId). There is no need to add CATEGORY to the FROM; you would need it only to filter on the name 'Electric bike'.
cinema.+passages: Customers and bikes are not linked directly: a customer makes rentals (RENTAL), and each rental includes bikes (RENTAL_LINE). Both tables are needed in the FROM, even though none of their columns is displayed.
cinema.+select: Why DISTINCT? A customer appears once per electric bike rented: without DISTINCT, you get 16 rows for only 11 different customers.
cinema.+jointures.3: Four tables, three joins, one per arrow followed: CUSTOMER → RENTAL → RENTAL_LINE → BIKE. If you forget one, every row is combined with every row of the other table (Cartesian product).

questions.enonce: Display, without duplicates, the last name and first name of the customers who have rented at least one electric bike (category number 2).
variantes: INNER JOIN RENTAL ON CUSTOMER.CustomerId = RENTAL.CustomerId
INNER JOIN RENTAL_LINE ON RENTAL.RentalId = RENTAL_LINE.RentalId
INNER JOIN BIKE ON RENTAL_LINE.BikeId = BIKE.BikeId
questions.indice: Follow the arrows of the diagram: CUSTOMER → RENTAL → RENTAL_LINE → BIKE (three join conditions). A customer who rented several electric bikes must appear only once: DISTINCT.

questions.enonce: Display, for each store (store name), the number of rentals recorded, from the busiest store to the quietest.
variantes: INNER JOIN RENTAL ON STORE.StoreId = RENTAL.StoreId
questions.indice: « For each store » means GROUP BY. The store name is in STORE, the rentals are in RENTAL.

cinema.+jointures: Strictly speaking, RENTAL alone would be enough to count the rentals of each customer number: the join with CUSTOMER is there only to display the last name.
cinema.+groupe: Group by `CUSTOMER.CustomerId`, not only by LastName: two customers with the same last name would otherwise be merged into one group. LastName is added to the GROUP BY because it is displayed.
cinema.+groupe.2: « At least 3 » translates as `>= 3`. The condition is on a count, which only exists after grouping: it cannot go in the WHERE.
cinema.+resultat: Check: 8 customers. Campbell (no. 4) is the most loyal, with 5 rentals; the 7 others have exactly 3, so `> 3` would keep only him.

questions.enonce: Display the customers (number, last name) who have made at least 3 rentals, with their number of rentals.
variantes: INNER JOIN RENTAL ON CUSTOMER.CustomerId = RENTAL.CustomerId
questions.indice: A condition on a computed number (COUNT) goes in HAVING, after GROUP BY. CustomerId exists in two tables: say which one (CUSTOMER.CustomerId).

cinema.+tables: Only CUSTOMER columns are displayed: RENTAL appears only inside the subquery, not in the main FROM.
cinema.+filtres: « Never » is answered in two steps: the subquery lists the customers who **do** have a rental, then NOT IN keeps the others. A join with RENTAL cannot do it: a join only produces rows for customers who have rentals.
cinema.+resultat: Check: 10 customers out of 25, including Rhys Morgan (no. 25), whom you will delete in the Updates. Variant accepted: `NOT EXISTS (…)`, with the condition `R.CustomerId = C.CustomerId` inside the subquery.

questions.enonce: Display the customers (number, last name, first name) who have never rented a bike.
questions.indice: « Never »: NOT IN (a subquery that lists the customers who have at least one rental).

cinema.+tables: ReferredBy is a foreign key that points to **the same table**: the referrer is also a customer. To show the customer's name and the referrer's name on the same row, CUSTOMER must appear twice in the FROM.
cinema.+alias: Choose aliases that tell the role: C for the customer, R for the referrer. Without them, `LastName` would be ambiguous: SQL could not tell which copy you mean.
cinema.+jointures: The direction matters: `C.ReferredBy = R.CustomerId` means « R is the one who referred C ». Reversed (`R.ReferredBy = C.CustomerId`), the two names swap roles.
cinema.+resultat: Check: 15 rows. The 10 customers referred by nobody (empty ReferredBy) do not appear: the join finds no match for them. Taylor referred three customers, so that name appears three times in the last column.

questions.enonce: Display each customer who was referred by another customer: last name and first name of the customer, and last name of the customer who referred them.
variantes: SELECT C.LastName, C.FirstName, R.LastName AS Referrer
INNER JOIN CUSTOMER R ON C.ReferredBy = R.CustomerId;
questions.indice: The CUSTOMER table is linked to itself (ReferredBy points to another customer). Use it twice in the FROM with two aliases: C (the customer) and R (the referrer).

questions.enonce: The bikes of rental no. 1036 have just been brought back today (15 June 2025): record the return date.
questions.verif: SELECT * FROM RENTAL ORDER BY RentalId
questions.indice: UPDATE table SET column = value WHERE condition. Without WHERE, every rental would be modified. NOW() returns the date of the day.

questions.enonce: PedalPoint adds a new category: « Tandem », number 7, with a standard daily rate of 45. Add it.
questions.verif: SELECT * FROM CATEGORY ORDER BY CategoryId
questions.indice: INSERT INTO table VALUES (value1, value2, …) in the order of the columns of the table.

cinema.+table: DELETE removes whole rows: no column list, no SET. Customer no. 25 can be deleted because no other row refers to him: he has no rental and has referred nobody.
cinema.+ciblage: Always target by the **primary key** (`CustomerId = 25`): a condition on the name could delete several customers. Without a WHERE, DELETE would empty the whole table.
cinema.+resultat: Second part: deleting customer no. 4 (Ross Campbell) is refused. He has 5 rentals (RENTAL.CustomerId) and referred customers no. 5 and 10 (CUSTOMER.ReferredBy): deleting him would leave rows pointing to a customer who no longer exists. This is **referential integrity**.

questions.enonce: Customer no. 25 (Rhys Morgan), who has never rented a bike, asks for his account to be deleted. Delete him. Then try to delete customer no. 4: what happens, and why?
questions.verif: SELECT * FROM CUSTOMER ORDER BY CustomerId
questions.indice: DELETE FROM table WHERE condition. Customer no. 4 has rentals (and referred other customers): referential integrity refuses the deletion, because RENTAL.CustomerId and CUSTOMER.ReferredBy refer to him.

cinema.lecture:
I go through the statement rule by rule, looking for the two objects linked and the number in each direction:
- « All the bikes of a given model have the same brand and the same category »: brand and category depend on the **model**, not on the individual bike. Today they are repeated in every bike of the same model.
- « record the list of models once (model code, model name, brand, category) »: a new object → new table **MODEL**. A model has one category, a category covers several models → one-to-many → foreign key #CategoryId in MODEL.
- « each bike being of one model »: a bike has one model, a model is shared by several bikes → foreign key #ModelId in BIKE; Model, Brand and CategoryId leave BIKE.
- « Each accessory has a code, a name and a daily price »: a new object → table **ACCESSORY**.
- « which accessories were taken and in what quantity; the same accessory can be part of many rentals »: a rental includes several accessories, an accessory appears in several rentals → many-to-many, with a quantity for each pair → link table **RENTAL_ACCESSORY**.
cinema.retraits: Model, Brand and CategoryId leave BIKE. The reason is **redundancy**: these three pieces of information depend on the model, so they are repeated for every bike of that model, with a risk of contradiction (two bikes of the same model with different brands). They move to MODEL, where they are written only once.
cinema.+entites: The accessory is described by its own information (code, name, daily price): it is an object in its own right. Its daily price belongs to the accessory, not to a rental.
cinema.+entites.2: The trap: creating MODEL but leaving CategoryId in BIKE. Every bike of a model has the same category, so the category belongs to the model: #CategoryId goes in MODEL, and a bike finds its category through its model (BIKE → MODEL → CATEGORY).
cinema.+liens: The foreign key goes in BIKE, on the « many » side: one model, many bikes. A list of bike numbers in MODEL would require several values in one cell.
cinema.+associations: The trap: adding #AccessoryId in RENTAL. A rental could then include only one accessory, with no quantity. Since a rental can include several accessories, and an accessory several rentals, you need a link table with one row per (rental, accessory) pair.
cinema.+associations.2: Composite key: RentalId alone is not enough (a rental has several accessories), nor is AccessoryId alone. The quantity depends on both: it goes in RENTAL_ACCESSORY, neither in RENTAL nor in ACCESSORY.

questions.enonce: PedalPoint wants to improve its database. 1) All the bikes of a given model have the same brand and the same category: the company wants to record the list of models once (model code, model name, brand, category), each bike being of one model. 2) Customers can now add accessories to a rental (helmet, lock, child seat, panniers…). Each accessory has a code, a name and a daily price. For each rental, the company records which accessories were taken and in what quantity; the same accessory can of course be part of many rentals. Update the schema below.

tables.role: describe each bike model once (name, brand, category)
describe the accessories that can be rented
record the quantity of each accessory taken in a rental
describe each bike model once (name, brand, category)
describe the accessories that can be rented
record the quantity of each accessory taken in a rental

variantes.partiel: Almost: MODEL is created, but the category stayed in BIKE. Since every bike of a model has the same category, the category belongs to the model: CategoryId must move from BIKE to MODEL.

questions.indice: Information that depends on the model and not on the individual bike (brand, category) moves to a new table, and BIKE keeps only a foreign key to it. A « many-to-many » relationship (rentals ↔ accessories) becomes a table whose primary key combines the keys of the two linked tables, and which carries the quantity.

questions.enonce: Interview with Sarah Jenkins, store manager at PedalPoint: « Customers book their bikes on our website. When a booking request comes in, the website checks whether a bike of the requested category is available on those dates. If one is available, the booking is confirmed; if not, the booking is refused and the customer is told so straight away. On the day, the customer comes to the store counter. We hand over the bike only when the booking is confirmed and the customer has either paid a deposit or shown a PedalPoint member card — members don't pay a deposit. When the bike is brought back, the counter staff inspect it. If it is in good condition, the deposit is refunded. If it is damaged, the deposit is kept and a repair request is sent to the workshop, which repairs the bike and puts it back in service. » Draw the event-driven process chart (events, operations, synchronisations) of this process.

attendus.synchronisation: Booking confirmed AND (Deposit paid OR Member card shown)

nodes.label: Availability check
actions: Check bikes of the category on the dates

autoevaluation: The four actors are present: the customer, the website, the store counter and the workshop.
The availability check, on the website, has two emission rules: bike available (booking confirmed) / no bike available (booking refused).
The bike handover waits for the booking confirmed AND (the deposit paid OR the member card shown): this is the synchronisation.
The return inspection, triggered by the bike returned, has two cases: good condition (deposit refunded) / damaged (deposit kept and repair request).
The workshop repair is triggered by the repair request and puts the bike back in service.
questions.indice: First identify the actors (lanes), then what triggers each operation. An operation that leads to two different situations has two emission rules. The handover needs several things at the same time, one of them in two possible forms: that is where a synchronisation with a condition combining « and » and « or » is needed.
